site.tagline: Moss, stone and gravel gardens, designed and kept by a small studio.

categories.description: Growing, planting, pressing in and keeping moss.

posts.title: Pressing in new moss, piece by piece
posts.excerpt: Moss is not laid like turf. It is pressed in by hand, a palm at a time, and then left alone.
posts.content:
We grow our moss in shallow trays at the studio for a year before it goes into a garden. When it is ready we break it into pieces the size of a palm and press each one into damp soil, edge to edge, so there is no gap for weeds.

Then comes the hard part: leaving it alone. New moss needs water, shade and no feet for six weeks. We put a small bamboo edge around it and a note on the veranda.

posts.title: Why we never use a leaf blower
posts.excerpt: A blower clears the leaves in a minute and the moss with them. A bamboo rake takes longer and leaves the garden whole.
posts.content:
Moss holds on by threads finer than hair. The air from a leaf blower lifts the leaves and, a little at a time, the moss underneath. After a few autumns the garden is patchy and nobody knows why.

We clear leaves with soft bamboo rakes and our hands, twice in November. It is slower, and quieter, and it is the best hour of the year in most gardens.

posts.title: Setting a stone a third deep
posts.excerpt: A stone that sits on the ground looks placed. A stone set a third into it looks as if it has always been there.
posts.content:
Our stone setter turns every stone several times before choosing its face. Then a third of it goes below the surface, on a bed of crushed stone so it never sinks or tilts.

It feels wasteful to bury the part you paid for. But it is the buried third that makes the visible two thirds look calm.

posts.title: Raking gravel the evening before a tea gathering
posts.excerpt: Straight lines from the gate, rings around the basin, and no footprints after the last stroke.
posts.content:
At the Hoshi Tea Garden we rake the gravel the evening before every gathering. Straight lines run from the gate; around the water basin they become rings, like water around a dropped stone.

The trick is to rake yourself out of the garden backwards, so the last stroke is the one by the gate.

posts.title: Letting moss sleep through August
posts.excerpt: Brown moss in summer is usually resting, not dying. Water early, shade what burns, and wait for September.
posts.content:
Many owners call us in August because their moss has turned brown. Most of the time it is simply dormant: moss closes up in the heat and opens again with the first cool rain.

Water before seven in the morning, never in the midday sun, and keep feet off it. By the end of September it will be green again.

posts.title: One maple is enough
posts.excerpt: In a small courtyard, one well-placed Japanese maple gives you all four colours of the year.
posts.content:
Fresh green in April, deep green in summer, red in November and fine grey branches in winter. One maple, kept low and open, changes a courtyard more than any planting plan.

We place it where it can be seen from the room you sit in most, and prune it every February so the light still reaches the moss below.
